cards.title: A token is not a word
bullets: Models read text as tokens: a word, a piece of a word, or punctuation.
Cost and context are counted in tokens, not in the words you see on the page.
Rare names and code identifiers split into more pieces, so they are easier to misspell back.
cards.takeaway: Budget tokens, not words. The model never sees the letters the way you do.

cards.title: Next-token prediction is the whole trick
bullets: An LLM is trained to guess the next token given everything so far.
Helpful answers fall out of that habit, plus later instruction tuning.
It is not looking up a stored fact. It is continuing a pattern that often happens to be true.
When the pattern is thin, it continues anyway. That continuation is a hallucination.
cards.takeaway: Treat the model as a fluent completer. Ask it to show the steps you can check.

cards.title: One token goes around the block
cards.body: The prompt is already a list of tokens. Each block mixes them, then the model scores the next token and appends the one it samples.
cards.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  P[Prompt tokens] --> B[Transformer blocks]
  B --> N[Next-token scores]
  N --> S[Sample one token]
  S --> P
cards.takeaway: Generation is a loop: read the tokens you have, append one, repeat.

cards.title: An agent is a model in a loop
bullets: The model proposes the next step. A tool does something the model cannot do alone.
The tool result comes back as text the model can read on the next turn.
Stop when the goal is met, a step budget runs out, or the same action repeats.
cards.takeaway: The model decides. The tool acts. The observation is just more text.

cards.title: Write the stop condition first
bullets: A loop without a stop will spend the step budget on near-duplicate actions.
Good stops are observable: a test passed, a file exists, the user confirmed.
If the model cannot tell success from the tool output, it will keep going.
cards.takeaway: Define done in a way a tool result can prove. Do not leave done to a vibe.

cards.title: Goal, tool, observation, stop
cards.body: Each lap either returns to planning with a new observation or exits because the stop check passed.
cards.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  G[Goal] --> P[Plan]
  P --> T[Tool]
  T --> O[Observation]
  O --> C{Stop?}
  C -->|No| P
  C -->|Yes| D[Done]
cards.takeaway: If you cannot point at the stop check, you do not have an agent yet. You have a retry.

cards.title: Keep the request path stateless
bullets: Any app instance should be able to serve the next request.
Session data, files, and queues live in a store the instances share.
When one instance dies, the load balancer sends the next request somewhere else.
cards.takeaway: If a user is stuck to one machine, that machine is now a single point of failure.

cards.title: Name the limit before you draw boxes
bullets: A design that does not say requests per second and a latency budget is a sketch.
The slowest synchronous hop on the path decides the user's wait.
Move work that can finish later onto a queue, and keep the request for the answer they are waiting on.
cards.takeaway: Put a number on the path. Then decide what is allowed to be slow.

cards.title: One request, four hops
cards.body: The client only waits on the app. The app reads the database for the answer and hands slower work to the queue.
cards.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> L[Load balancer]
  L --> A[Stateless app]
  A --> D[(Database)]
  A --> Q[Queue]
cards.takeaway: Draw the synchronous path separately from the work you are willing to finish later.
